div.p: Fixed-priority with preemption threshold (FPPT) is an important form of real-time scheduling algorithm, which fills the gap between fixed-priority preemptive (FPP) and fixed-priority non-preemptive (FPNP). However, this scheduling scheme together with the requirements of fault tolerance makes the prediction of a real-time system's behaviors more difficult than traditional scheduling scheme. The major contribution of this work is twofold. First, we present an appropriate schedulability analysis, based on response time analysis, for supporting fault-tolerant FPPT scheduling in hard real-time systems. The errorrecovery techniques are considered to be used to carry out fault tolerance. Second, we propose the optimal priority assignment algorithm which can be used, together with the schedulability analysis, to improve system fault resilience.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Fixed-priority preemptive (FPP) scheduling algorithms [1] and fixed-priority non-preemptive (FPNP) scheduling algorithms [2] are two important classes of real-time scheduling algorithms. To obtain the benefits of both FPP and FPNP algorithms, there are several other algorithms trying to fill the gap between them. The fixed-priority with preemption threshold (FPPT) scheduling algorithm [3] is one of them. Under FPPT, each task has a pair of priorities: regular priority and preemption threshold, where the preemption threshold of a task is higher than or equal to its regular priority. The preemption threshold represents the task's running-time preemption priority level. It prevents the preemption of the task from other tasks, unless the preempting task's priority is higher than the preemption threshold of the current running task. Saksena and Wang have shown that task sets scheduled with FPPT can have significant schedulability improvements over task set using fixed priorities [3]. The regular priority of a task can be predefined or obtained by algorithms [2], but the preemption threshold is usually calculated during a schedulability analysis [3] [4]. All preemption thresholds of a task set form a preemption threshold assignment or assignment for simplification. If an assignment can make each task schedulable by FPPT, the assignment is called valid.

This paper extends the current work on FPPT in [3] by importing a fault tolerant scheme in FPPT scheduling. The ability to tolerate faults is an extremely desired characteristic for safety-critical hard real-time systems. However, the implementation of fault-tolerance increases the complexity of keeping the system computation complying with the requirements specification. Effective schedulability analysis, which takes the fault model, fault tolerance mechanisms and the scheduling algorithm into consideration, is needed to guarantee the timeliness property. In this paper, an algorithm to analyze the schedulability of fault-tolerant FPPT (FT-FPPT) scheduling is provided. In order to improve the fault resilience of systems, another algorithm to calculate the optimal preemption threshold assignment for robustness to faults is also presented.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the assumed computation model. The related work is introduced in Section 3. Section 4 presents our approach to carrying out the schedulability analysis for FT-FPPT. In Section 5, the method for finding out the optimal priority assignment is given. Finally, the conclusion is made in Section 6.

div.head: Computational Model
div.p: We assume that there is a set S = { 1 ,…, n } of n tasks, called primary tasks, that must be scheduled by the system without any errors. The jth job of task i is denoted as J i , j . The index, j, for jobs of a task is started from zero. The duration between the time when a job enters a system and when it finishes is called the response time of the job. The worst-case response time of a task is equal to the maximal response time of all of its job in the lifetime of a system. Any primary task i in S has a period, T i , a deadline, D i , and a worst-case computation time, C i . Tasks can be periodic or sporadic. For sporadic tasks, the period means the minimum inter-arrival time. We assume that (a) the tasks are independent, i.e., there is no blocking due to shared resource, (b) tasks do not suspend themselves, except at the end of their execution, and (c) the overheads due to context switching, etc., are negligible (i.e., assumed to be zero). Each primary task will also be given a regular priority [1, ] i n π ∈ and a preemption threshold [ , ] i i n γ π ∈ . We assume that larger number denotes higher priority, and that no two tasks have the same regular priority. An assignment of preemption threshold can be denoted as = { 1 , 2 ,…, n }.

Each primary task i can have some alternative tasks associated with it. Each alternative task corresponds to a given action taken to recover i from a given error. Any alternative task has a worst-case computation time called worst-case recovery time. To simplify the task model, we assume that all alternative tasks associated with i run at the same preemption threshold as i . Hence, we do not include the details of individual alternative task per primary hereafter in the description. We only need to refer to the alternative task with the longest worst-case recovery time in case of errors in task i . We use a i to denote this alternative task and CA i to denote its worst-case recovery time.

We assume that errors are detected in the task level. When an error interrupts the execution of a task, the system must schedule an appropriate alternative task, which is responsible for carrying out the errorprocessing procedure and has to finish before the deadline of its primary task. If errors take place in the alternative tasks, we assume that it is scheduled again for re-execution. We also assume that there is no cost associated with any scheduling of primary or alternative tasks. Further, we assume that all errors are detected by the system and faults only affect the results produced by the executing task.

The kinds of fault with which we are dealing are those that can be treated in the task level. It may be possible to use techniques such as exception handling or recovery blocks to perform appropriate recovery actions, modeled here as alternative tasks. In order to analyze the response time of tasks when errors may occur in their executions, we assume that there is a minimum interval between two consecutive error occurrences, T E . The minimum tolerable value of T E is important information about the system's fault resilience. With this value, designers can infer how likely the system will be subject to missed deadlines due to faults in a given environment. It is very important to improve fault resilience for the robustness of the systems. We use the magnitude of T E to measure this resilience in this paper, since the scheduling of a system to reduce T E will improve the resilience of the system, regardless of the actual fault model employed by the application engineer [4].

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Wang and Saksena's schedulability analysis [3] is based on the response time analysis of each task. The worst-case response time analysis is an extension of the level-i busy period analysis [5], in which the response time is calculated by determining the length of busy period, starting from a critical instant. However, their schedulability test is incorrect [6], as it may not consider all jobs in the first level-i busy period. The reason why all jobs must be checked is that the first job of a task in the first level-i busy period may not get the worst-case response time for the task. The corrected schedulability analysis was presented by Regehr [6] and the WCRT of a task i can be calculated through the following equations:

div.p: The response time of a task i consists of three parts: (a) i 's computation time (C i in the worst case). (b) interference time from other higher or equal priority tasks, including previous instances of the same task, denoted as I i . (c) blocking time from lower priority tasks caused by the preemption threshold, denoted as B i .

Based on the schedulability analysis, Wang and Saksena also provide an algorithm to assign preemption thresholds [3], which is claimed to be optimal. Jiongxiong Chen et al. [7] have found that when a task set is schedulable by FPPT, there may exist multiple valid preemption threshold assignments. All valid assignments form a solution space that is delimited by minimal and maximal assignment. The assignment proposed in [3] is proved to be the minimal assignment, and the algorithm to compute the maximal assignment from an existing valid assignment is given in [8].

For fault-tolerant scheduling, a study done by Burns, Davis and Punnekkat [9] provides schedulability tests for fault tolerant task sets scheduled with FPP. Based this work, Lima and Burns [10] studied the approach to run the recovery of tasks with higher priorities and provided an effective schedulability test to guarantee the predictability of system with this character. Based on the test, Lima and Burns also provide a method to find out the optimal priority configuration, which maximizes the fault resilience of task sets [4]. As far as we know, the scheduling issue of FT-FPPT has never been studied before.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis for FT-FPPT
div.p: In this section, we will discuss the schedulability analysis for FPPT considering the fault model and fault-tolerant mechanism described in Section 2. The schedulability analysis method for FT-FPPT is proposed by extending the algorithm proposed in [3] [6]. In order to calculate the effect of the faulttolerance mechanism to FPPT, we modify the calculation of task response times to include errorinduced additional recovery processing time. During a time interval t, the additional recovery time due to errors is denoted as E t .

Under the assumption of fault-tolerant mechanism given in Section 2, the effects of an error can be eliminated by immediately executing a job of an alternative task at its preemption threshold priority level. Errors may interrupt the execution of a task more than once. As the worst-case period of error occurrence is T E , the maximum number of errors that may take place during a time interval t can be presented as / E t T . These errors may occur in the execution of any task executed during t. Accordingly, the error recovery time of all these tasks will contribute to E t . div.head: Preemption Threshold Assignment Search Method
div.p: The optimal priority assignment is the assignment that can tolerate the minimum interval between consecutive error occurrences. A description of the method to find out the optimal preemption threshold assignment regarding the analysis described earlier is given in this section. The regular priority assignment of a task set is assumed predefined, which can be conducted by algorithms [2]. Before searching for the optimal preemption threshold assignment, we need a method to calculate the minimum value of T E for a given assignment such that the system is still schedulable.

div.head: Optimal Assignment of Preemption Threshold
div.p: An intuitive method to compute the optimal assignment of preemption threshold is to calculate T e for each possible valid preemption threshold assignment. Since i is larger than or equal to i , there will be n! possible assignments in the search space. If the time complexity to calculate R' i is assumed to be O(r), where r is not constant and depends on the task set, regular priority, and preemption threshold, then the computational complexity to obtain the optimal assignment will be O(n!*r).

To decrease the computational complexity, we can take the following two measures: (a) Reducing the search space of possible preemption threshold assignments. (b) Reducing the starting value scope of the branch and bound search when compute the T e for a given assignment.

In [3], some interesting properties are presented, which will help us to reduce the search space for finding the robust preemption threshold assignment. Although these properties are proposed for FPPT, they still hold true for FT-FPPT.
Lemma 1: Changing the preemption threshold of task i from 1 to 2 may only affect the worst case response time of task i and those tasks whose regular priorities are between 1 and 2 .

Proof: Changing the preemption threshold of task i will change its interference time from higher priority tasks. Therefore, the response time of task i will be affected. Corollary 1: The worst-case response time of task i will not be affected by the preemption threshold assignment of any task j with j > i . Lemma 2: With given priority i , if setting the preemption threshold i equal to the highest priority in the system can not make a specific task i schedulable, then the task set is unschedulable.

Proof: From Equation 10, it can been seen that the preemption threshold reduces the worst-case response time of low priority task i by preventing the interference from some higher priority tasks after i starts execution, thus improving its schedulability. Setting the preemption threshold of i to the highest priority in the system will avoid the interference from higher priority tasks and the fault-induced additional processing time will remain the same (see Equation 8), thus give the maximum reduction to the worst-case response time of i . If i is still not schedulable, since the priority is predefined, there is no way to make it schedulable. Furthermore, the task set will also be unschedulable.

When a task set is schedulable, the research work in [3] presents an algorithm to find a valid assignment which starts its computation with i = i for 1 i n, i.e., from FPP, therefore, denoted as MinFromFPP (see Figure 2 in [3] for the pseudo-code). [11] has proved that the assignment obtained is minimal. The research work in [8] presents an algorithm to compute the maximal assignment provided that a valid assignment is already known, denoted as MaxFromMin (see Figure 4 in [8]). As min can be obtained through the MinFromFPP algorithm, of course it can be used to compute max .

Theorem 2 shows that any valid assignment must be delimited by the minimal and maximal assignments. Although [7] also provides several mechanisms to generate valid assignments, a mechanism to generate all valid assignments without checking all possible assignments delimited by the minimal and maximal assignment is still unknown. Therefore, we need to check all the possible assignments delimited by the minimal and maximal assignments to obtain an optimal assignment for the robustness of systems.

The search of the optimal assignment can be conducted through a nested algorithm shown in Figure 2. The first input parameter S is a task set with a predefined regular priority assignment. The second input parameter i is the number of a task in S which is to be assigned a new preemption threshold. The initial value of i is zero, which denotes the first task in S. The algorithm Search traverses all the possible assignments between the minimal and maximal assignments in a nested manner. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we have addressed the problem of providing suitable schedulability analysis for FT-FPPT scheduling algorithm. Two major contributions have been presented. First, response time analysis for FT-FPPT with a given priority assignment has been described. Second, an efficient algorithm that assigns the optimal preemption threshold configuration has been presented to maximize the fault resilience of a task set. Presently, the FPPT scheduling algorithms have been confined to the applications in uniprocessor systems. In our ongoing work, we are evaluating the usability of this scheduling scheme in multiprocessors systems, for the improvement of performance and robustness.
